query: Which material can be used for to improve the ductility and toughness of the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy (HEAs), and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing niobium (Nb) into an HfZrTi high-entropy alloy will improve its ductility and fracture toughness compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast HfZrTi-based high-entropy alloy with an initially equimolar or near-equimolar composition, exhibiting limited ductility and toughness.
generation.intervention: Add varying Nb contents (e.g., 5–15 at.%) to the HfZrTi alloy via arc melting in an inert atmosphere, followed by standard homogenization heat treatment.
generation.conditions: Process the HfZrTi–Nb alloys under identical fabrication conditions (same melting and cooling rates) to isolate the effect of Nb content on microstructural and mechanical properties.
generation.structural_mediator: Possible phase stabilization of a ductile BCC matrix and reduction of crack initiation sites upon Nb addition.
generation.mechanism: Niobium additions can promote a ductile phase, refine microstructure, and hinder crack propagation, leading to improved fracture resistance and tensile ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable increase in strain-to-failure (ductility) and fracture toughness without a substantial loss in strength, relative to Nb-free HfZrTi alloys.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties (e.g., elongation and fracture toughness) of HfZrTi alloys without Nb doping.
generation.boundary: Beyond a certain Nb concentration (above ~15 at.%), additional brittle phases may form, reducing ductility. Exact optimal Nb content is undetermined due to limited data.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvement in ductility and toughness remains uncertain; no specific magnitude of the effect is confirmed by the provided data.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple HfZrTi alloy ingots with incremental Nb additions (0, 5, 10, and 15 at.%) using arc melting. Homogenize at a fixed temperature and time. Conduct X-ray diffraction, and microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM) to confirm phase constitution.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, total elongation, and fracture toughness.
Fractography to identify crack propagation paths and fracture features.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-doped HfZrTi alloy does not show any increase in elongation or toughness relative to the Nb-free baseline, or if detrimental phases form at all tested Nb levels, then the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. However, most of these RHEAs are generally characterized with high density and poor high temperature oxidation
